newsitem.title: CANADA: New Alberta 1997-98 budget has only minor changes.
newsitem.headline: New Alberta 1997-98 budget has only minor changes.

text.p: The Canadian province of Alberta, in a new budget following the Conservative government's re-election last month, on Monday projected a surplus in fiscal 1997-98 of C$154 million.
However, the surplus could be as high as C$750 million, if oil and natural gas prices and corporate taxes beat provincial assumptions, new provincial treasurer Stockwell Day said.

The budget, projecting Alberta's fourth straight annual surplus, featured only minor changes from the one delivered in February before Premier Ralph Klein's government won its second majority in the provincial legislature.
"Albertans saw this budget before the election campaign," Day said. "They knew what we planned to do with their hard-earned dollars and they supported the plan with an increased majority."
Jim Dinning, Day's predecessor, projected a 1997-98 surplus of C$144 million in his February budget.
In the new document, oil-rich Alberta revised downward its price forecast for benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude oil to US$18.50 a barrel from US$19.
The move reflected oil market fluctuations and dropping prices over the past few months, Day said, adding Alberta was maintaining its commitment to conservative forecasts.
The lower oil prices were expected to mean a drop in provincial revenues of about C$2 billion.
However, the surplus was expected to be C$10 million higher than previously projected because of lower debt servicing costs, Day said.
Alberta's annual interest costs have dropped by C$419 million since their peak in 1994-95, the province said. In February, the savings were pegged at C$389 million.
Day said Alberta's net debt was expected to fall to C$3.5 billion by March 1998, based on a revised 1996-97 surplus estimate of C$2.26 billion. The previous estimate for 1996-97 was C$2.23 billion.
Another change in the new budget was an increase of C$20 million in spending on health care to cover rising volumes and costs in province-wide services, Day said.
